verdict.rationale: The in-place-of pattern is dense and spans both testaments on three independent lexical tracks. The Hebrew preposition 'in place of' (tachat, H8478, 505 occurrences, core sense 'in place of') describes the ram offered as a burnt offering 'in place of' (tachat) Isaac's son in Genesis 22:13, the substitute victim. The Greek preposition 'in place of' (anti, G0473, 22 occurrences, attested sense 'in place of' or 'in exchange for', as in Matthew 2:22 and Matthew 5:38) stands in the ransom saying 'a ransom in place of many' (lytron anti pollon) in Mark 10:45 and Matthew 20:28, the tightest exchange idiom. The sin-bearing verbs 'to bear' (nasa, H5375) and 'to carry' (sabal, H5445) in Isaiah 53:4, 53:11 and Leviticus 16:22, with 'to cause to fall on' (paga, H6293) in the Hiphil causative form (the Hebrew causative form, meaning 'to cause to do') in Isaiah 53:6 (YHWH made the iniquity of all of us fall on him), and the Greek 'to bear up' (anaphero, G0399) in 1 Peter 2:24 and Hebrews 9:28 (he bore the sins of many), all place the guilt of the many onto one. The broader 'for' or 'on behalf of' (hyper) texts (Romans 5:8, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13, 1 Peter 3:18) confirm the same exchange where context supplies a one-for-many frame or a just-for-unjust antithesis.

scripture.force: Abraham offered up the ram ('ram', ayil, H0352) as a burnt offering ('burnt offering', olah, H5930) 'in place of' (tachat, H8478) his son. The token order in the source places 'in place of' (tachat) directly between the burnt offering and his son, which is the lexical signature of a substitute victim: an animal dies in the position the son was about to occupy. 'In place of' (tachat) occurs 505 times with a stable core sense of 'under', 'instead of', or 'in place of', so the in-place-of reading here is not strained.

The live goat 'bears' (nasa, H5375) upon itself all their 'iniquities' (avon, H5771) into a solitary land. The same verb 'to bear' (nasa) that Isaiah 53:4 uses of the Servant is here used of the substitute animal that carries the people's guilt away from them. The grammar attaches the bearing to the goat and the iniquities to the people, the lexical structure of transfer.

The corrective particle 'surely' (aken) opens it: surely it was our sicknesses he 'bore' (nasa, H5375) and our pains he 'carried' (sabal, H5445). The possessive suffixes mark the burdens as ours while the subject pronoun ('he', hu, H1931) marks the bearer as a distinct single person. The ETCBC clause data (a syntactic database of the Hebrew Bible) repeats Object functions for the burden nouns, confirming the Servant as the one who takes the others load.

'All of us' (kol, H3605, repeated as an inclusive frame opening and closing the verse) strayed like sheep, and YHWH 'caused to fall' (paga, H6293, parsed Hiphil perfect 3rd person masculine singular, that is, the Hebrew causative form denoting a completed past action performed by a single male subject) on him the 'iniquity' (avon, H5771) of all of us. The Hiphil ('the Hebrew causative form, meaning to cause to do') with the divine subject is the grammatical hinge of penal transfer: God himself lays the guilt of the whole group onto the single Servant, which forecloses a merely coincidental suffering reading.

He shall 'bear' (sabal, H5445) their 'iniquities' (avon, H5771). 'To bear' (sabal) occurs only nine times in the canon, and two of them are in this one Servant Song (here and in 53:4), with Lamentations 5:7 using it of bearing the iniquities of others. The narrow distribution clustered on guilt-bearing fixes the sense as carrying moral liability, not mere physical weight.

The Son of Man came to give his life a ransom 'in place of' many ('a ransom in place of many', lytron anti pollon). The source token order is 'ransom' (lytron, G3083), then 'in place of' (anti, G0473), then 'many' (pollon, G4183) in immediate sequence. 'In place of' (anti) is the Greek preposition whose core lexical sense is 'over against', 'instead of', 'in exchange for' (seen plainly in Matthew 2:22 of one ruler reigning in place of another and in Matthew 5:38 'eye for eye'), so 'a ransom in place of many' (lytron anti pollon) is the lexically tightest substitution idiom in the set: one life given in the stead of the many. Matthew 20:28 carries the identical phrase.

It is expedient that 'one' man (heis, G1520) die 'for' (hyper, G5228) the 'people' (laos, G2992) and the whole nation not perish. Here 'for' (hyper) alone is broad, but the numeral one set against the people supplies a one-instead-of-many structure: a single death stands in the place of the destruction owed to the group. The frame, not the bare preposition, carries the substitution.

He himself ('himself', autos) 'bore up' (anenenken, aorist [a completed past action] of 'to bear up' (anaphero, G0399)) 'our sins' (tas hamartias hemon) in his body onto the 'tree' (epi to xylon, G3586). 'To bear up' (anaphero) is the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) cultic term for carrying an offering up to the altar, attested that way in this same book and letter group (Hebrews 7:27, Hebrews 13:15, 1 Peter 2:5). Applied to sins lifted onto the cross it echoes Isaiah 53 'to bear' (nasa) and lands on healing by his 'wound' (molops). Our sins, his body: the structure of transfer.

Christ was offered once to 'bear' (anaphero, G0399) the 'sins' (hamartia, G0266) of 'many' (pollon, G4183). The token sequence sets the many as the genitive (the 'of-X' grammatical form) whose sins the one carries, the same one-bears-the-guilt-of-many shape as Isaiah 53:6 and Mark 10:45. 'To bear' (anaphero) here pairs with the cultic verb 'to offer' (prosphero) earlier in the verse, locking the sin-bearing into a sacrificial frame.

Christ suffered once concerning sins, 'just for unjust' ('the righteous for the unrighteous', dikaios hyper adikon, with 'righteous' (dikaios, G1342) set directly over against 'unrighteous' (adikos, G0094)), 'in order that' (hina) he might 'bring you to God' (prosagago). The 'for' (hyper) is here flanked by an explicit righteous-for-unrighteous antithesis, which is the clearest exchange formula: the one who is 'righteous' (dikaios) stands in the place of those who are 'unrighteous' (adikos), and the purpose clause names reconciliation. The antithesis, not 'for' (hyper) by itself, secures the substitution.

The one not knowing 'sin' ('the one not knowing sin', ton me gnonta hamartian, G0266) God made to be sin 'for us' (hyper hemon, G5228), 'in order that' (hina) we might become the 'righteousness' (dikaiosyne, G1343) of God in him. The double accusative (a noun in the direct-object grammatical form, used twice here) 'made-sin' sets up a deliberate interchange: his sinlessness and our sin trade places so his righteous standing transfers to us. 'For' (hyper) here sits inside the made-sin and become-righteousness exchange, which supplies the in-place-of force.

While we were 'still' (eti) 'sinners' ('we being sinners', hamartolon onton hemon, G0268) Christ 'died for us' ('died for us', hyper hemon apethanen, with 'to die' (apothnesko, G0599)). Read on its own this verse only states a death on behalf of the unworthy, since 'for' (hyper) can mean 'for the sake of' without exchange. The substitution sense it carries comes from the surrounding atonement texts (the one-for-many frame and the just-for-unjust antithesis), not from this clause by itself. This is the legitimate point where readers diverge.

Christ 'redeemed us' ('he bought us out', exegorasen, from 'to buy out' (exagorazo, G1805)) from the 'curse' (katara, G2671) of the law by 'becoming' (genomenos) a curse 'for us' (hyper hemon katara, G5228), citing the law that everyone hanged on a tree is cursed. The participle (a verbal adjective) 'becoming' (genomenos) plus 'for' (hyper) plus the predicate 'curse' (katara) is an exchange of status: he takes the cursed position so the curse is lifted from us. Commercial buy-out plus curse-transfer doubly encode substitution.

complicating_texts.resolution: The preposition 'for' or 'on behalf of' (hyper, G5228) is genuinely broad. Across its 151 occurrences it most often means 'on behalf of', 'for the sake of', or 'concerning' with no exchange in view (for example prayers offered 'for' (hyper) all people in 1 Timothy 2:1, affliction 'for' (hyper) your comfort in 2 Corinthians 1:6, was Paul crucified 'for' (hyper) you in 1 Corinthians 1:13). So 'for' (hyper) by itself does not prove that one party stands in the place of another. It is resolved because the canon supplies the in-place-of sense from other words and frames: the preposition 'in place of' (anti) in Mark 10:45 and Matthew 20:28, the Hebrew 'in place of' (tachat) in Genesis 22:13, the one-instead-of-many structure in John 11:50 and 2 Corinthians 5:14, and the explicit just-for-unjust antithesis in 1 Peter 3:18. Where 'for' (hyper) sits inside one of those frames it carries substitution; where it stands alone it carries only benefit. The atonement texts repeatedly supply the frame.

The first colon (our sicknesses and pains) is quoted in Matthew 8:17 of physical healing, which could narrow the bearing to disease rather than guilt. But Isaiah 53:5 to 53:6 immediately recast the same bearing in moral terms ('transgression', pesha, H6588; 'iniquity', avon, H5771; with 'to cause to fall' (paga, H6293) in the Hiphil (the Hebrew causative form, meaning 'to cause to do') placing guilt on him), and 53:11 says he shall 'bear' (sabal, H5445) their iniquities. The healing language is one facet of the bearing, not a competing reading; the lexical field is penalty-bearing for sin.

variants.note: No variant units were supplied in the bundle for the anchor verses, and the cited apparatus marks in the printed text (the raised dots in 1 Peter and 2 Corinthians) touch pronoun and word-order readings ('you' (hymas) versus 'us' (hemas), presence of the article 'the') that do not disturb the 'in place of' (anti), 'in place of' (tachat), 'for' (hyper), or sin-bearing-verb structure. The Hebrew anchors in Genesis 22, Leviticus 16, and Isaiah 53 are outside ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope. The verdict holds across the plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes 'in place of' (anti) in the ransom saying and 'in place of' (tachat) in Genesis 22:13 as lexicalized replacement, then reads the surrounding 'for' (hyper) and sin-bearing-verb texts in their light: one stands in the position of the many and dies the death they were owed. The 'righteous-for-unrighteous' (dikaios-for-adikos) antithesis of 1 Peter 3:18 and the made-sin interchange of 2 Corinthians 5:21 are read as exchange formulas, and Isaiah 53:6 'to cause to fall' (paga) in the Hiphil (the Hebrew causative form, meaning 'to cause to do') as God transferring guilt onto the Servant.

Stresses that 'for' or 'on behalf of' (hyper, G5228) lexically means 'on behalf of' or 'for the sake of' and does not by itself require strict exchange, as its many non-atonement uses show. On this reading the death is for the benefit of and as the representative of sinners, which is real and reconciling, while pressing it into a one-to-one penal swap is held to read more than the bare preposition states. This reading still affirms that Christ died for sinners in a way that reconciles them, the proposition under test, but is cautious about the exact mechanism. It is represented fairly here in its strongest form.

Reads the substitute victim of Genesis 22:13 (ram 'in place of' (tachat) the son) and the scapegoat of Leviticus 16:22 ('to bear' (nasa), bearing iniquities away) as types whose pattern of one-in-place-of-the-guilty is realized in the Servant of Isaiah 53 and in Christ. The typological chain itself carries the in-place-of force independent of any single New Testament preposition.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses affirm the proposition that Christ died for sinners in a reconciling way. They diverge on how strictly the mechanism is substitution, and the divergence tracks a real lexical fact: 'in place of' (anti) and 'in place of' (tachat) lexicalize replacement, while 'for' (hyper) lexicalizes benefit or representation and acquires replacement force only from a one-for-many frame or an antithesis. The Genesis-Leviticus-Isaiah-to-New-Testament arc is the load-bearing redemptive-historical link.

stem_audit.notes: The proposition states that Christ died for sinners in their place and that his death is, among other things, a substitute death by which those for whom he died are reconciled to God. The hedge 'among other things' keeps it from smuggling a single atonement theory label, and 'substitute death' plus 'in their place' is the very claim the lexis is then allowed to confirm or deny rather than a tradition-specific taxonomy. No neutralization is required. Verdict unchanged from the prior file: affirms true, high confidence. Key terms verified against live lexical-store counts ('in place of' (anti, G0473) 22, 'in place of' (tachat, H8478) 505, 'for' (hyper, G5228) 151, 'to bear' (nasa, H5375) 651, 'to carry' (sabal, H5445) 9, 'to bear up' (anaphero, G0399) 10, 'ransom' (lytron, G3083) 2) and against verified token sequences for Mark 10:45, Matthew 20:28, Genesis 22:13, Isaiah 53:6, John 11:50, 2 Corinthians 5:14, Hebrews 9:28, 1 Peter 2:24, 1 Peter 3:18, 2 Corinthians 5:21, Galatians 3:13.

lay_summary: The plain sense of the words points firmly toward substitution: Christ dying in the place of sinners so that they are brought back to God. Two words carry 'in place of' as their own meaning. The Greek 'in place of' (anti), used of one ruler reigning in place of another and of 'eye for eye', appears in the ransom saying where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom in place of many ('a ransom in place of many', lytron anti pollon), the tightest exchange phrase in the canon. The Hebrew 'in place of' (tachat), a very common word meaning 'under' or 'instead of', describes the ram offered up as a burnt offering in place of Abraham's son, a substitute victim. Alongside these run the bearing verbs. In Isaiah 53 the Servant 'bears' (nasa) and 'carries' (sabal) burdens the speakers call ours, and verse six uses a causative form ('to cause to fall', paga, in the Hiphil, which is the Hebrew causative form meaning 'to cause to do') to say God made the iniquity of us all fall on him, a transfer of guilt onto one person. The scapegoat 'bears' (nasa) the people's iniquities away in Leviticus, using the same verb. In the New Testament he 'bore up' (anaphero) our sins in his body onto the tree, and he was offered to 'bear' (anaphero) the sins of many, using a word that elsewhere means to lift an offering onto the altar. There is one honest place where readers diverge, and it comes straight from the words. A third preposition, 'for' (hyper), appears in many of these texts, but 'for' (hyper) by itself only means 'on behalf of' or 'for the sake of'. It is used of praying for people and of suffering for someone's comfort, where no one stands in anyone else's place. So a death described only as 'for' (hyper) sinners proves that it was for their benefit, not by itself that it was instead of them. What settles the matter is that the canon does not leave 'for' (hyper) alone. It pairs it with the numeral one set against many, as in one man dying for the people, and with a blunt antithesis, the just for the unjust ('the righteous for the unrighteous', dikaios hyper adikon), and with the exchange where the sinless one is made sin so that we become 'righteousness' (dikaiosyne). In those frames 'for' (hyper) carries the same in-place-of force that 'in place of' (anti) and 'in place of' (tachat) carry on their own. So the case rests on 'in place of' (anti) and 'in place of' (tachat) and the bearing verbs, with 'for' (hyper) joining them wherever the surrounding words supply a one-for-many or just-for-unjust frame. The pattern is dense, it spans law, prophets, gospels, and letters, and it survives the manuscript variants, so the lexical case for substitution is strong while the exact mechanism is where careful readers still differ.

license_audit.non_redistributable_reason: Two sources carry CC-BY-NC-4.0 and cannot be redistributed in bulk: MACULA-Greek (used for the verified token sequences of Mark 10:45 'a ransom in place of many' (lytron anti pollon) and Hebrews 9:28 'bearing sins' (anaphero hamartias)) and ETCBC-BHSA (used for the Isaiah 53 clause and function data). The verdict itself can be re-derived from the redistributable OSHB, STEPBible, MorphGNT, and TSK citations if a publishable subset is required, since the 'in place of' (anti) idiom and the 'in place of' (tachat) substitute-victim are recoverable from those sources.
